name: Personal Attack
definition: Attacking the person instead of addressing their argument.
examples: "Tomato says my blade matches the cuts in the missing carrot. But look at his bruised skin—why trust someone that rotten?"
"Tomato claims he saw me spill the soup. He can't even decide whether he's a fruit or a vegetable, so how could he identify the culprit?"

name: Bandwagon
definition: Claiming something is true because many people believe it.
examples: "Chef, every utensil in the drawer believes Tomato stole the salt. They can't all be wrong!"
"The forks, spoons, and knives all agree that gadgets make better witnesses than produce. You should believe my testimony over Tomato's."

name: Appeal to Pity
definition: Using sympathy in place of relevant evidence.
examples: "Please don't find me guilty of shredding the recipe, Chef. My handle is cracked, and I've already had such a difficult week!"
"If you rule that I ruined the soup, I'll be thrown into the junk drawer. You wouldn't make me spend the rest of my life alone in the dark, would you?"

name: Irrelevant Authority
definition: Treating someone's opinion as proof when they lack relevant expertise.
examples: "The refrigerator's ice dispenser says Tomato stole the flour. It's an expert at making ice, so its judgment about theft must be correct."
"The famous cake-decorating mixer says these scratches came from Tomato. Winning decorating contests makes it an expert in scratch identification!"

name: False Dilemma
definition: Presenting only two choices when other possibilities exist.
examples: "Chef, either you find Tomato guilty of spilling the oil, or you're saying that spilling oil on the floor is acceptable."
"Either Tomato stole the recipe, or I did. And I certainly didn't!" (Other kitchen residents also had access.)

name: Hasty Generalization
definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from too little evidence.
examples: "One tomato rolled off the counter yesterday. That proves tomatoes can't control where they go, so this Tomato must have rolled into the cake."
"Tomato got one detail wrong about breakfast. Everything he says about the missing butter must be false."

name: Straw Man
definition: Distorting someone's argument to make it easier to attack.
examples: Tomato: "The peeler should be kept in a protective cover." Peeler: "Tomato wants every gadget locked away forever so nobody can cook!"
Tomato: "The crumbs on Toaster don't prove he stole the bread." Toaster: "Tomato thinks we should ignore all physical evidence!"

name: Red Herring
definition: Introducing an irrelevant issue to distract from the original question.
examples: "Tomato asks why there's frosting caught in my whisk wires. But Chef, shouldn't we be discussing how filthy the oven is?"
"Before we discuss whether my cord knocked over the milk, let's talk about Tomato leaving seeds all over your cutting board."

name: Whataboutism
definition: Deflecting criticism by pointing to someone else's similar wrongdoing.
examples: "Tomato accuses me of dripping grease onto the recipe. But he dripped juice onto the shopping list yesterday!"
"Why should I answer Tomato's accusation that I blocked the sink? Tomato clogged the drain with his sticker last week!"

name: Circular Reasoning
definition: Using the conclusion itself as support for the conclusion.
examples: "My account of the missing cheese is accurate because I'm a reliable grater. You can tell I'm reliable because my account is accurate."
"Tomato stole the basil because he's the thief in this kitchen. How do I know he's the thief? Because he stole the basil."

name: Appeal to Ignorance
definition: Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false, or vice versa.
examples: "Tomato can't prove he never entered the pantry last night. Therefore, he entered it and stole the sugar."
"Nobody has proved that my blades caused the scratches on the counter. That proves I'm innocent."

name: False Cause
definition: Assuming that because one event followed another, the first caused the second.
examples: "The soup curdled immediately after Tomato rolled beside the stove. His arrival must have curdled it!"
"The kitchen lights went out just after Tomato accused me. His accusation must have caused the power failure!"

name: Slippery Slope
definition: Claiming one step will lead to an extreme outcome without enough support.
examples: "If you let Tomato keep that stolen basil leaf, next he'll take a whole bunch, then empty the pantry, and soon there won't be a single ingredient left!"
"If Tomato is allowed to question my testimony, every ingredient will start questioning every gadget. Soon the kitchen will be in chaos and dinner will never be served!"

name: False Analogy
definition: Treating two things as equivalent despite differences that matter.
examples: "Chef, you throw away empty tomato cans. This Tomato has no filling inside him either, so you should throw him away too!"
"You unplug a blender when it makes too much noise. Tomato is making noise by objecting, so you should silence him for the rest of the trial."

name: Equivocation
definition: Switching between different meanings of the same word during an argument.
examples: "Chef said we need a sharp witness. My blades are sharp, so my testimony must be the most intelligent."
"Tomato admitted he was ripe for an argument. Ripe means ready, so he admitted he was ready to start the fight!"

name: Loaded Question
definition: Asking a question that assumes an unproven claim.
examples: "Tomato, where did you hide the measuring spoon you stole?" (It hasn't been established that Tomato stole it.)
"Have you stopped sneaking into the refrigerator after midnight?" (Either yes or no accepts that Tomato previously did this.)

name: Cherry-Picking
definition: Selecting evidence that supports a claim while ignoring relevant evidence against it.
examples: "This camera image shows Tomato beside the broken plate!" (The gadget skips the next frame, which shows its own cord pulling the plate off the counter.)
"The salt shaker heard Tomato threaten to 'crush' Garlic!" (Ignores the rest of the conversation: Tomato was reading the chef's recipe aloud.)

name: Moving the Goalposts
definition: Changing the standard of proof after the original standard has been met.
examples: "Show us a photo proving you were in the fruit bowl when the spill happened." Tomato provides one. "A photo isn't enough. Now you need a video!"
"I'll accept your innocence if one witness confirms you never touched the oven." The kettle confirms it. "Actually, I'll need three witnesses—and none of them can be appliances."
